mappings.note: Names the phloem as the tissue that carries food away from the leaves: identification of a tissue.

Sets xylem against phloem on what each carries and in which direction: two tissues differentiated by structure and function. The printed answer text belongs to the Krishna sunlight item and is reported as a defect.
Decides which of Vani's four set-ups will show starch by checking which requirement each one lacks: reading a controlled experiment.
The oxygen half of the same experiment, answered the same way.
The snail is respiring and so adding carbon dioxide: naming the process an organism is carrying out.
The water plant in light is photosynthesising and so using carbon dioxide. The printed answer belongs to the net-gas-exchange item and is reported as a defect.
Kamala Sohonie and her doctoral work on plant respiration: a scientist's story.
Completes the products column for photosynthesis and respiration, which is the pair of word equations LO-135 names.
Losing all photosynthesisers would cut off the base of food chains and the oxygen supply: the role of the process argued out.
Food made in the leaves and carried to the tuber by phloem: the process traced across the plant.
The broad flat blade gives area for light and for stomata: form tied to its effect on the process.

Identifies what Krishna's light-against-dark comparison is testing, which is reading the design of an investigation. Its printed answer belongs to the xylem-and-phloem item and is reported as a defect.
All living parts of a plant respire, day and night: a process stated for the whole organism.
Oxygen in and carbon dioxide out during plant respiration: the gas exchange of the process. Not LO-135, since no equation is required.
Respiration exists to release usable energy from glucose: the purpose of the process.
Lime water turns milky because the germinating seeds are giving off carbon dioxide: the observation traced to its cause. Not LO-132, because the set-up is given and only the reason is asked.
Picks the correct respiration word equation, with glucose and oxygen in and carbon dioxide, water and energy out.
Photosynthesis and respiration contrasted on which gas each uses and releases: two processes set side by side.
Net uptake of carbon dioxide and release of oxygen by day, since photosynthesis outpaces respiration. The printed answer belongs to the water-plant item and is reported as a defect.
Assigns glucose, oxygen and water to X, Y and Z in the respiration equation.
The two processes keeping atmospheric gases in balance: the cycle explained.
A sealed bottle garden survives because the plant's two processes recycle each other's gases: the same cycle applied to a closed system.
Matches inputs to outputs for both processes, which is the pair of equations in prose form.
Water and minerals travelling from root to leaf through xylem: the transport step of the plant's processes.
Sunlight as the energy source for photosynthesis, one of the process's requirements.
The stem, carrying its own answer, is again the energy-source question and is mapped on that; the printed answer is a tissue-matching key and is reported as a defect.
Matches carbon dioxide, water, sunlight and glucose to their roles in photosynthesis: the raw materials and product of the process.
Matches each classic experiment to the requirement it proves: the item is about what the evidence shows, so the investigation outcome.
Matches leaves, respiration, photosynthesis products and xylem to their descriptions: process knowledge across the chapter.
Names sunlight as the second factor the pot experiment shows to be essential: a conclusion from the comparison.
Starch as the storage form of plant food, an output of the process.

Whichever half is read, the stem on food storage or the printed answer on the snail-and-plant carbon dioxide balance, the item sits on the plant life processes; the misalignment is reported as a defect.
Assertion and reason swap the jobs of xylem and phloem, so the item turns on telling the two tissues apart.

Why a gardener or farmer must supply water, light and minerals: the life processes applied to growing plants in practice. Not LO-134, because the item asks for the practical reason rather than the mechanism.
Requires two experiments described with set-up, procedure, observation and conclusion: investigation work throughout.
Explains the whole of photosynthesis, site, inputs, energy, pigment and products (LO-134), and then asks for the word equation (LO-135).
How a plant runs both processes and manages the gas exchange between them: two processes explained together.
Defends the food-factory description of leaves by the structures and the process inside them.
Reads the three-plant case study to say what has happened to the unwatered plant and what it lacks: inference from a controlled comparison.
Predicts the iodine result for covered and uncovered parts of a leaf and states what the experiment proves.
The stem, again self-answering, is the covered-leaf experiment and is mapped on that; the printed answer is a photosynthesis-and-respiration comparison table and is reported as a defect.
Describes the transport system and what xylem and phloem each do: the movement of substances through the plant explained. Not LO-130, because the item asks for description rather than contrast.
Stomata, their guard cells and the two processes they serve: structure explained through the processes it enables.
What destarching is and why it must come first: the logic of preparing a plant for the experiment.
Traces carbon dioxide through the stomata and water up from the roots to the photosynthesising cells: the raw materials followed through the process.
